    Generating noise¶

    Noise is a row-wise perturbation of the observed values: each affected row gets its own random deviation, drawn independently (in contrast to drift, where one systematic shift is applied to all affected rows). Use noise to make a pipeline robust to measurement error, sensor jitter, or rounding — the signal is still there, but each observation is a bit off.

    This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

    1. Acting on the observation process — add noise directly to the observed values (AdditiveNoiseGenerator, GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator). These generators do not use a DGP and nothing propagates: the value is changed exactly where the noise lands.
    2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — inject noise at a node of a fitted causal model and let it propagate to the descendants (CausalNoiseGenerator).

    Both accept a selector to decide which rows are affected (see the Understanding badgers notebook for the selector contract).

    Goal¶

    Corrupt values with additive noise: per-class white noise, noise drawn from any scipy distribution, and noise injected into a causal graph with descendants recomputed.

    In [1]:
    Copied!

from numpy.random import default_rng
from scipy.stats import norm
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator, GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator

rng = default_rng(seed=0)

    Load and prepare data¶

    We first load an existing dataset from sklearn.datasets. The class values are stored as a column of X, so plotting uses the explicit vector cls.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    X, y = make_blobs(centers=4, random_state=0, cluster_std=0.25)
# classes are a column of X
Xc = np.column_stack([X, y])
column_mapping = {'f0': 0, 'f1': 1, 'cls': 2}
cls = Xc[:, column_mapping['cls']]   # explicit class vector for plotting
print(X.shape, '->', Xc.shape)
    X, y = make_blobs(centers=4, random_state=0, cluster_std=0.25) # classes are a column of X Xc = np.column_stack([X, y]) column_mapping = {'f0': 0, 'f1': 1, 'cls': 2} cls = Xc[:, column_mapping['cls']] # explicit class vector for plotting print(X.shape, '->', Xc.shape)

    Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶

    Add noise to all values¶

    AdditiveNoiseGenerator adds a draw from distribution to every cell of X — each row gets its own independent deviation.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    # norm(scale=0.25): an ABSOLUTE scale -- every cell gets an N(0, 0.25) draw,
# independent of the column's own std. Contrast with the sigma-relative
# noise_std of the causal generator in Part B.
gen = AdditiveNoiseGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), distribution=norm(scale=0.25))
print('shape:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)
# verify: the std of each column grew by exactly the noise std
std_before = X.std(axis=0, ddof=0)
std_after = Xt.std(axis=0, ddof=0)
print('std before:', np.round(std_before, 3))
print('std after :', np.round(std_after, 3))
assert np.allclose(std_after, np.sqrt(std_before**2 + 0.25**2), atol=0.05)
    # norm(scale=0.25): an ABSOLUTE scale -- every cell gets an N(0, 0.25) draw, # independent of the column's own std. Contrast with the sigma-relative # noise_std of the causal generator in Part B. gen = AdditiveNoiseGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), distribution=norm(scale=0.25)) print('shape:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape) # verify: the std of each column grew by exactly the noise std std_before = X.std(axis=0, ddof=0) std_after = Xt.std(axis=0, ddof=0) print('std before:', np.round(std_before, 3)) print('std after :', np.round(std_after, 3)) assert np.allclose(std_after, np.sqrt(std_before**2 + 0.25**2), atol=0.05)

    Add noise per class¶

    GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator combines two independent parameters that are easy to confuse:

    • the selector decides which rows receive noise. It returns one boolean mask (or deficit probability) per class value. In the demo below, {0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.} means: every row of every class affected with probability 1 — so all rows are noisy. Set a value to 0.5 and half of that class's rows would be noisy (Bernoulli-wise); set it to 0. and that class stays clean.
    • noise_std_per_class decides how strong the noise is on the affected rows, per class: {0: 0.1, 1: 0.2, 2: 0.3, 3: 0.4} makes class 3 rows four times noisier than class 0 rows. It has no effect on which rows are noisy.

    In short: selector = who is affected, noise_std_per_class = how badly.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, ClassSelector

# WHO is affected: every row of every class is affected (probability 1.0)
# columns: f0=0, f1=1, cls=2 ? selectors take int positions
selector = ClassSelector([0, 1], class_column=2,
                         proportions={0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.}, rng=rng)

# HOW BADLY: noise std per class value (only applies to affected rows)
gen = GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(Xc.copy(), selector=selector,
                  noise_std_per_class={0: 0.1, 1: 0.2, 2: 0.3, 3: 0.4})
print('shapes equal (values changed):', Xt.shape == Xc.shape)
    from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, ClassSelector # WHO is affected: every row of every class is affected (probability 1.0) # columns: f0=0, f1=1, cls=2 ? selectors take int positions selector = ClassSelector([0, 1], class_column=2, proportions={0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.}, rng=rng) # HOW BADLY: noise std per class value (only applies to affected rows) gen = GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(Xc.copy(), selector=selector, noise_std_per_class={0: 0.1, 1: 0.2, 2: 0.3, 3: 0.4}) print('shapes equal (values changed):', Xt.shape == Xc.shape)

    Copied! 
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise.causal import CausalNoiseGenerator
import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise.causal import CausalNoiseGenerator import dowhy.gcm as gcm from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP def make_scm(graph): scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph) for node in graph.nodes: if not list(graph.predecessors(node)): scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution()) else: scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel( prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor())) return scm

    Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶

    CausalNoiseGenerator injects noise at a node of a fitted causal model. The noise perturbs the node's value, and the change cascades to the descendants through the structural equations: descendant = f(new parent values) + fresh noise. Only downstream nodes are affected; upstream nodes and untouched rows stay as they were.

    Copied!

    1. Build the causal graph¶

    We use a three-node chain X -> Y -> Z. The node names are symbolic; a column_mapping maps them to column positions of X.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    # --- Build the chain X -> Y -> Z ---
chain = nx.DiGraph()
chain.add_edges_from([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")])

draw_graph(chain, title="Chain: X → Y → Z")
plt.show()
    # --- Build the chain X -> Y -> Z --- chain = nx.DiGraph() chain.add_edges_from([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")]) draw_graph(chain, title="Chain: X → Y → Z") plt.show()

    2. Generate data from the DAG¶

    Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

    Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

    3. Fit the DGP¶

    The GcmSCMDGP adapter wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel: every non-root node's mechanism is a linear AdditiveNoiseModel fitted on the original data, root nodes resample the observed values. The SCM is built with dowhy-gcm's own API (see the make_scm helper).

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(make_scm(chain), column_mapping).fit(X.copy())

gen = CausalNoiseGenerator(random_generator=np.random.default_rng(0), dgp=dgp)
    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(make_scm(chain), column_mapping).fit(X.copy()) gen = CausalNoiseGenerator(random_generator=np.random.default_rng(0), dgp=dgp)

    # verify the propagation contract
# X is upstream of the perturbed node Y: untouched
assert np.allclose(Xt[:, 0], X[:, 0])
# Y received row-wise noise: larger scatter, same shape
print('std of Y: %.3f -> %.3f' % (X[:, 1].std(ddof=0), Xt[:, 1].std(ddof=0)))
assert Xt[:, 1].std(ddof=0) > X[:, 1].std(ddof=0)
# Z is a descendant of Y: recomputed (values changed)
assert not np.allclose(Xt[:, 2], X[:, 2])

    

    # verify the propagation contract
# X is upstream of the perturbed node Y: untouched
assert np.allclose(Xt[:, 0], X[:, 0])
# Y received row-wise noise: larger scatter, same shape
print('std of Y: %.3f -> %.3f' % (X[:, 1].std(ddof=0), Xt[:, 1].std(ddof=0)))
assert Xt[:, 1].std(ddof=0) > X[:, 1].std(ddof=0)
# Z is a descendant of Y: recomputed (values changed)
assert not np.allclose(Xt[:, 2], X[:, 2])

    Expanding rows (n_copies)¶
    Set n_copies > 1 to expand the data: each original row produces
n_copies noisy copies. Shape grows (appending mode).
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [19]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    Xt_exp = gen.generate(
    X.copy(),
    selector=AlwaysSelector([1]),
    n_copies=3,
    noise_std=0.5,
)
print(f"expanded shape: {Xt_exp.shape}  (from {X.shape[0]} rows)")
_ = plot_2panel(X, Xt_exp, x_name='X', y_name='Y')

    

    Xt_exp = gen.generate(

    • Noise is row-wise: each affected row draws its own deviation —
in contrast to drift, where one systematic shift hits all rows.
      • 

    • selector = who is affected (masks/probabilities per class),
noise_std_per_class = how strongly (magnitude per class).
      • 

    • Causal noise mutates X in place — pass X.copy() to keep the
original.
      • 

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Takeaways¶
      

    • Shape is preserved: noise changes values only, never the row count.
      • 

    • AdditiveNoiseGenerator adds raw draws from any frozen scipy distribution; the scale is absolute (pass per-column scales yourself).
      • 

    • Causal noise recomputes descendants of the perturbed nodes via the DGP — the defect spreads through the graph.
      •
